text: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as four decimal octets, like 192.168.1.10. Every address splits into a network portion and a host portion, and the subnet mask is what tells a device exactly where that split happens — ones mark the network portion, zeros mark the host portion.

CIDR notation writes the subnet mask as a slash plus the number of network bits — 192.168.1.10/24 means the same thing as a 255.255.255.0 mask. This is how you'll see addresses written in almost every router command, config file, and cloud console.

Take 192.168.1.0/26 — 6 host bits means 64 total addresses per block. The network address, 192.168.1.0, identifies the subnet itself. The broadcast address, 192.168.1.63, reaches every host on it. Neither is ever assignable to a device — the usable range is .1 through .62.

Subnetting isn't just about not wasting addresses. It's a core security tool: placing servers, workstations, and guest or IoT devices in separate subnets lets you apply different firewall rules and different monitoring to each group, instead of one flat network where anything can reach anything.
Next lesson: IPv6 addressing fundamentals — the 128-bit address space built to outlast IPv4's exhaustion, and the notation differences you'll need to read it correctly.
